title: Commit half a file: splitting one messy edit into two clean commits
summary: You fixed a bug and reformatted the file in the same sitting. Split them apart with hunk-level staging so the bug fix is reviewable on its own.
mental_model: The index is not file-granular. `git add -p` walks the diff hunk by hunk and lets you stage some and not others — the same mechanism as `git apply --cached` on a hand-edited patch, which is what this scenario uses so it can run without an interactive prompt.

steps.title: Look at the two unrelated changes
steps.why: One diff, two ideas: a validation fix near the top, a logging-format tweak at the bottom. Committing them together means a reviewer cannot approve one without the other.
steps.expect: Two separate hunks in one file.

steps.title: Count the hunks git sees
steps.why: `@@` markers delimit hunks. Git will happily stage them independently — the file is not the unit of staging, the hunk is.
steps.expect: Two @@ blocks — the units git can stage separately.

steps.title: Stage only the bug fix
steps.why: `git add -p` would ask 'Stage this hunk?' for each one and you would answer y then n. Here the same thing happens non-interactively: cut the first hunk into a patch and apply it to the index only.

write.content:
--- a/dosing.py
+++ b/dosing.py
@@ -4,6 +4,8 @@
 
 
 def dose(ml):
+    if ml <= 0:
+        raise ValueError('dose must be positive')
     return ml * RATE

steps.expect: Only the validation lines are staged. The logging change is untouched.

verify.label: the logging change is NOT staged

steps.title: Commit the fix on its own
steps.why: This commit does exactly one thing. It can be reviewed in ten seconds, cherry-picked to a release branch, or reverted without dragging cosmetics along.

steps.title: Commit the rest
steps.why: What remains in the working tree is the logging tweak. One more commit and the same edit session has produced two honest commits instead of one muddled one.

steps.title: Check the split is real
steps.why: Each commit touches one concern. `git log -p` reads like a story rather than a dump, and `git bisect` can actually localise a regression to one of them.

verify.label: the edit became two commits on top of the original
verify.hint: stage the fix hunk alone, commit, then commit the rest

verify.label: the first commit holds the bug fix
…and nothing else
verify.hint: stage only the first hunk before committing

verify.label: the second commit holds the logging change
the working tree is clean, patch file included

pitfalls: `git add -p` keys: y stage, n skip, s split into smaller hunks, e edit the hunk by hand, q quit. `s` and `e` are what make it powerful.
After partial staging, the working-tree file still has everything. Never assume the tests you ran locally reflect what you staged — `git stash -k` runs them against the staged version.
`git commit -a` after partial staging swallows the hunks you deliberately left out.
`git restore -p` and `git stash -p` use the same hunk picker for discarding and stashing.
